missions/lausanne-movement/name: Post-war evangelical missions (Billy Graham, Lausanne 1974, unreached peoples, 10/40 window)
missions/lausanne-movement/statusNote: The Lausanne Movement continues as a global network; Lausanne 4 met in Seoul-Incheon in September 2024 and issued the Seoul Statement. Its leadership and participation are now predominantly from the global South, though American funding and agendas remain influential and debates over social responsibility, sexuality and strategy continue.
missions/lausanne-movement/summary: After 1945 conservative evangelicals, increasingly estranged from the ecumenical movement, built their own global mission networks around Billy Graham, Christianity Today and new agencies. The Wheaton and Berlin congresses of 1966 led to the International Congress on World Evangelization at Lausanne in July 1974, whose Covenant, drafted by John Stott, reaffirmed the priority of evangelism while confessing evangelical neglect of social responsibility. Ralph Winter’s call to reach ‘hidden’ or unreached peoples and later the ‘10/40 window’ reshaped evangelical strategy.
missions/lausanne-movement/story:
Post-war American evangelicalism, organised in the National Association of Evangelicals (1942) and its Evangelical Foreign Missions Association (1945), alongside the older Interdenominational Foreign Mission Association (1917), sent a flood of missionaries into the world after the Second World War — many of them veterans who had seen Asia and Africa during the war. Billy Graham’s crusades, from Los Angeles (1949) and Harringay in London (1954) to New York (1957), Australia (1959) and Seoul (1973, where over a million attended the final service on Yoido Plaza), made him the movement’s public face. Christianity Today (1956), Fuller Theological Seminary (1947) and agencies such as World Vision (1950) and Campus Crusade for Christ (1951) built an evangelical infrastructure that consciously stood apart from the World Council of Churches.

Two congresses in 1966 marked the separation. The Congress on the Church’s Worldwide Mission at Wheaton College (April 1966), sponsored by the IFMA and EFMA, issued the Wheaton Declaration, which criticised the WCC’s theological pluralism and universalism while confessing evangelical failures in social concern and cooperation. The World Congress on Evangelism in Berlin (October–November 1966), convened by Christianity Today with Carl F. H. Henry as chair and Graham as honorary chair, gathered some 1,200 delegates from about 100 countries under the theme ‘One Race, One Gospel, One Task’. Regional congresses followed in Singapore (1968), Minneapolis (1969), Bogotá (1969) and Amsterdam (1971), widening participation from the global South.

The International Congress on World Evangelization met at the Palais de Beaulieu, Lausanne, from 16 to 25 July 1974, with about 2,700 participants from some 150 countries, nearly half from the global South. Ralph Winter’s address argued that most non-Christians — some 2.7 billion people — lived in ‘hidden peoples’ with no church able to evangelise them by near-neighbour witness, so that cross-cultural mission remained essential. The Latin Americans René Padilla and Samuel Escobar delivered plenary papers criticising an evangelicalism tied to American culture, consumerism and the ‘American way of life’, and calling for a gospel that addressed poverty and injustice; about 500 participants signed a ‘Theology and Implications of Radical Discipleship’ statement. The Lausanne Covenant, drafted by a committee chaired by John Stott, stated (paragraph 5) that ‘evangelism and socio-political involvement are both part of our Christian duty’ and expressed penitence for having sometimes regarded them as mutually exclusive, while affirming (paragraph 6) that ‘in the church’s mission of sacrificial service evangelism is primary’. Paragraph 9 addressed the moratorium debate from Bangkok, accepting that ‘a reduction of foreign missionaries and money in an evangelized country may sometimes be necessary’ to promote the national church’s growth in self-reliance.

The balance between evangelism and social action continued to divide the movement. Graham, Winter and Donald McGavran wanted the Lausanne Committee for World Evangelization (formed 1974) to focus on evangelism; Stott, Padilla, Escobar and others insisted on the Covenant’s wider vision. The 1977 Pasadena consultation on the homogeneous unit principle, the Willowbank consultation on gospel and culture (1978), the Consultation on World Evangelization at Pattaya (1980) — where a group of participants protested the neglect of social issues — and the Grand Rapids consultation on Evangelism and Social Responsibility (1982), which described social action as a consequence of, bridge to and partner of evangelism, each worked through the tension. Latin American evangelicals of the Fraternidad Teológica Latinoamericana (1970) developed ‘misión integral’, later carried into the Micah Network (1999). Lausanne II in Manila (1989) produced the Manila Manifesto and launched the AD2000 and Beyond Movement, in which Luis Bush popularised the ‘10/40 window’ (1990) — the band from 10° to 40° north of the equator from West Africa to East Asia containing most unevangelised peoples.

The unreached-peoples paradigm, institutionalised in Winter’s U.S. Center for World Mission (Pasadena, 1976), the Perspectives course and the Joshua Project database, redirected evangelical sending toward Muslim, Hindu and Buddhist peoples and encouraged ‘insider movements’ and church-planting movements. Its critics argued that it reduced mission to managerial targets, used military metaphors, encouraged spiritual-warfare ‘mapping’ of territorial spirits (questioned by a Lausanne statement in 1993) and provoked hostility in countries sensitive to proselytism. Lausanne III at Cape Town (2010), with over 4,000 participants from 198 countries, issued the Cape Town Commitment, drafted largely by Christopher Wright, which framed mission in terms of love for God, neighbour and creation. Lausanne 4 in Seoul-Incheon (2024) issued the Seoul Statement, whose sections on human sexuality and other matters were criticised by some as narrowing the movement’s agenda.

Historians such as Brian Stanley see Lausanne as the moment when evangelicalism became a global, rather than Anglo-American, movement, with majority-world voices reshaping its theology. Its achievements include a broadly accepted evangelical statement of mission and a lasting network; its weaknesses include dependence on Western money, recurrent tensions between strategists and theologians, and an emphasis on quantifiable ‘closure’ that some see as eroding the Covenant’s holistic vision.
missions/lausanne-movement/beliefs/0: The uniqueness and universality of Christ and the necessity of personal faith for salvation, against universalism and religious pluralism
missions/lausanne-movement/beliefs/1: The authority and infallibility of Scripture as the basis for mission (Lausanne Covenant §2)
missions/lausanne-movement/beliefs/2: Evangelism is primary in the church’s mission, yet socio-political involvement is also a Christian duty (§5–6)
missions/lausanne-movement/beliefs/3: The task remains unfinished while ‘unreached’ or ‘hidden’ people groups have no viable church
missions/lausanne-movement/beliefs/4: The gospel must be contextualised but cultures are to be tested by Scripture (§10, Willowbank 1978)
missions/lausanne-movement/beliefs/5: Integral mission (misión integral): word and deed belong together (Padilla, Escobar, Micah Network)
missions/lausanne-movement/strategies/0: Mass evangelistic crusades and broadcasting (Billy Graham Evangelistic Association, Hour of Decision)
missions/lausanne-movement/strategies/1: Global congresses and consultations producing covenants and occasional papers
missions/lausanne-movement/strategies/2: People-group research and prioritisation (unreached peoples, 10/40 window, Joshua Project)
missions/lausanne-movement/strategies/3: Mobilisation courses and centres (U.S. Center for World Mission, Perspectives)
missions/lausanne-movement/strategies/4: Partnership with national evangelical fellowships and the World Evangelical Fellowship (later Alliance)
missions/lausanne-movement/strategies/5: Relief and development agencies (World Vision, Tearfund) linked to evangelical churches
missions/lausanne-movement/groupsReached: Conservative Protestants worldwide who were alienated from the WCC
Evangelical leaders of the global South, notably Latin America, Africa and Asia
Muslim, Hindu and Buddhist peoples targeted as ‘unreached’
University students through Campus Crusade, IFES and allied ministries
Mass audiences at crusades in Britain, the US, Korea, Africa and India
Pentecostal and charismatic churches increasingly drawn into evangelical networks
missions/lausanne-movement/challenges/0: Persistent disagreement over the relationship between evangelism and social action
missions/lausanne-movement/challenges/1: Balancing Western funding and leadership with majority-world ownership
missions/lausanne-movement/challenges/2: Political pressures: anti-communism, US foreign policy associations, and suspicion in Asian and Arab states
missions/lausanne-movement/challenges/3: Diversity among evangelicals (Reformed, Pentecostal, Anabaptist) over theology and methods
missions/lausanne-movement/challenges/4: Anti-conversion legislation and persecution in target regions
missions/lausanne-movement/challenges/5: Fragmentation of initiatives into competing networks after AD2000
missions/lausanne-movement/harms/0: Close association of some leaders with American political power and Cold War agendas, compromising perceived independence
missions/lausanne-movement/harms/1: Target- and statistics-driven strategies (the 10/40 window, ‘closure’) criticised as managerial and militaristic
missions/lausanne-movement/harms/2: Neglect or delay in confronting racism and apartheid, which the Covenant itself confessed
missions/lausanne-movement/harms/3: Spiritual-mapping and territorial-spirit practices in AD2000-era networks that stigmatised other religions and cities
missions/lausanne-movement/harms/4: Aggressive targeting of unreached peoples sometimes endangered local Christians and strained interfaith relations
missions/lausanne-movement/developments/: The Lausanne Covenant became the most widely used evangelical statement on mission
Gave majority-world theologians (Padilla, Escobar, Kato, Bediako) a global platform
Restored social responsibility to evangelical mission thinking after decades of reaction against the ‘social gospel’
Mobilised new missionary sending from Korea, Brazil, Nigeria and India
Promoted linguistic and ethnographic research on people groups
Built lasting networks for theological education, Bible translation and church planting
missions/lausanne-movement/outcome: Lausanne turned post-war evangelicalism into a global missionary network and a counterpart to the WCC. Its Covenant’s compromise — evangelism primary, social responsibility a duty — remained contested, but majority-world evangelicals increasingly set the movement’s direction.

missions/lausanne-movement/disagreements: Rejected the WCC’s perceived universalism and its definition of salvation as humanisation at Uppsala (1968) and Bangkok (1973); accepted the moratorium only partially (Covenant §9).
Padilla, Escobar and others criticised the homogeneous-unit principle and numerical pragmatism at Lausanne and Pasadena (1977).
missions/lausanne-movement/deviations/0: Strategy-driven programmes such as AD2000 drifted from the Covenant’s holistic vision toward quantitative targets
missions/lausanne-movement/deviations/1: Some networks adopted spiritual-warfare practices that Lausanne’s own 1993 statement questioned
